title: A Journey Through the Absurd Hell of Trump’s Third-Country Deportations
gist: Wired follows Pheap Rom, a Cambodian refugee and US green-card holder deported after a 15-year sentence not to Cambodia but to a prison in Eswatini, which took up to 160 US deportees for $5.1 million. The case illustrates how the Trump administration's third-country deportation policy (deals with ~35 nations, 25,000 people removed) rests partly on bureaucratic error, is spreading to Europe and the UK, and faces a Supreme Court legality hearing in December.

insights.claim: Under the second Trump administration, deporting immigrants to countries where they have no ties went from a rare, tightly restricted practice to a signature mass-removal policy, with deals signed with some 35 nations over two years.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Third-country removal deals are now a durable tool of US foreign policy and aid diplomacy.
insights.quote: Over the past two years, the administration has inked deals with some 35 nations to accept third-country deportees from the US.

insights.claim: DHS general counsel James Percival publicly stated the US had deported 25,000 people to third nations, the most comprehensive figure yet on the practice.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Gives a hard baseline for tracking the policy's scale.
insights.quote: we have deported 25,000 illegal aliens to third nations
insights.locator: In September, during one of those brief

insights.claim: Some third-country deportation destinations, including the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Sudan, are on the US State Department's 'Do Not Travel' list.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Reputational and legal exposure for the policy rises with destination risk.
insights.locator: Some of the other destination countries

insights.claim: Eswatini agreed to accept up to 160 US deportees for a $5.1 million payment, which its finance minister confirmed receiving and said would go to the National Disaster Management Agency; the memorandum of understanding was signed May 14, 2025.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Shows the per-head pricing (~$32,000 per slot) poorer states accept to host US deportees.
insights.quote: Eswatini’s finance minister confirmed that he had received a $5.1 million payment from the US
insights.locator: In November 2025, more than a month

insights.claim: The Eswatini deal was reportedly brokered in February 2025 by US embassy head Caitlin Piper and Prime Minister Russell Dlamini with the king's approval; the State Department would not say who signed the MOU, whose US signature has no printed name.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Opacity of deal terms is a target for litigation and congressional investigation.
insights.quote: the king embraced the deal as Eswatini’s contribution to world order
insights.locator: How Rom and the others came to be trapped

insights.claim: Eswatini, Africa's last absolute monarchy, has banned political parties since 1973, killed 46 people in a 2021 pro-democracy crackdown, has the world's highest HIV prevalence, and is described by the US State Department as having significant human rights issues.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: US reliance on such partners raises human rights and governance risk for the program.
insights.locator: Eswatini, a country about the size of New Jersey

insights.claim: Detainees argue that moving people across borders in exchange for payment amounts to trafficking, while being held in a prison despite committing no crime in Eswatini and paying for basics themselves.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Framing deportation deals as paid trafficking could drive legal challenges.
insights.quote: You are moving people around, and money is exchanged
insights.locator: This payment disclosure led the men

insights.claim: The Southern Africa Litigation Centre and other groups challenged the Eswatini deportation agreement as unconstitutional; the initial case was dismissed and an appeal went to Eswatini's Supreme Court in March.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Local court challenges are a channel that could disrupt receiving-country deals.

insights.claim: Pheap Rom, a Cambodian refugee born in a Thai refugee camp, appears to have been sent to Eswatini because US officials wrongly thought he should go to Thailand and never contacted Cambodia, which says the US did not reach its embassy before his removal.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Undercuts the US claim that every third-country removal followed due process.
insights.quote: his own country never even appears to have been asked

insights.claim: Rom's lawyer Tin Thanh Nguyen says Cambodia has accepted deportees for more than two decades, issues travel documents responsively, and moved to fix Rom's case within a week of being contacted, suggesting third-country removal was unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Evidence that some third-country removals stem from US process failures rather than refusal by home countries.

insights.claim: Immigration agents allegedly mocked deportees' requests for 'reasonable fear' interviews and only pretended to record them, according to Rom.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Due-process allegations feed the pending Supreme Court case.

insights.claim: Under US immigration law since the 1990s, legal permanent residents convicted of 'aggravated felonies' can lose their status and be deported after serving their sentences, a practice advocates call 'double punishment'.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Explains why long-time green-card holders form a large pool for removal.
insights.locator: Under US immigration law since the 1990s

insights.claim: Five EU countries announced in November plans to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, Italy has sent asylum seekers to Albania, and the UK sent an asylum seeker to Eswatini who later died.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Offshore migration processing is becoming a multi-country Western policy trend, creating payment flows to poorer host states.
insights.locator: Rather than slowing down in the face of resistance

insights.claim: Lawyer Tin Thanh Nguyen predicts that if the US keeps getting away with third-country expulsions, more wealthy countries will pay poorer nations to take their unwanted migrants.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Watch for more bilateral pay-for-deportation deals between rich and poor states.
insights.quote: This is going to be the new model for the West, not only for the United States

insights.claim: Federal courts have at least twice ordered DHS to stop third-country removals over insufficient due process, and both times the Supreme Court quickly let the administration resume; the Supreme Court will hear oral arguments on the practice's ultimate legality in December.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: The December Supreme Court hearing is the key catalyst for whether the program continues at scale.
insights.locator: The fate of all third-country deportees

insights.claim: Eswatini has received 32 US deportees in total, including a fourth batch of 11; only two have been freed, Rom to Cambodia and Orville Isaac Etoria to Jamaica.
insights.speaker: Timothy McLaughlin
insights.so_what: Low repatriation rates show detainees can be held indefinitely in third countries.
insights.quote: Thirty-two have been forced to the country in total.
insights.locator: Once a week, Rom calls the deportees
